title: Impacts of Artificial Lighting on Human Behaviour In-Office Buildings—A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Mohamed Salaheldin Amin Mohamed and Eziaku Onyeizu Rasheed, 2024
central_proposition: Optimized artificial lighting, particularly LED lighting with appropriate correlated color temperature (CCT), glare reduction, color rendering index (CRI), and illuminance, significantly enhances worker productivity, well-being, and cognitive performance in office environments by influencing circadian rhythms, emotional responses, and visual comfort.

concept_definitions.name: Artificial Lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Fluorescent and LED lighting, the primary types of artificial lighting significantly influencing workers' productivity due to their common usage in-office buildings.

concept_definitions.name: Human Behaviour
concept_definitions.definition: Workplace behaviour, including actions, interactions, and attitudes displayed by individuals within a professional setting.

concept_definitions.name: Productivity
concept_definitions.definition: Enhancing task performance, reducing errors, and influencing cognitive workloads.

concept_definitions.name: Mood and Emotional Well-Being
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting's impact on mood regulation is a vital component of workplace behaviour.

concept_definitions.name: Health and Wellness
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting's role in supporting circadian rhythms, preventing health issues, and reducing fatigue is a critical aspect of workplace behaviour.

concept_definitions.name: Correlated Colour Temperature (CCT)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of warmth or coolness in lighting.

concept_definitions.name: Colour Rendering Index (CRI)
concept_definitions.definition: The most utilized and globally recognized measure for evaluating colour quality.

concept_definitions.name: Glare
concept_definitions.definition: Glare factors, such as contrast and luminance.

concept_definitions.name: Dynamic Lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting capable of mimicking natural light patterns.

argument_structure: The paper systematically reviews existing empirical research on artificial lighting in office buildings, categorizing findings by lighting type (fluorescent vs. LED) and impact area (productivity, mood, health). It synthesizes these findings to draw conclusions about mechanisms and identifies research gaps for future investigation.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Artificial lighting influences human behavior through several mechanisms: regulating circadian rhythms (via spectral composition and dynamic patterns affecting melatonin), modulating emotional responses (via CCT and lighting types), enhancing cognitive engagement (via appropriate illumination for focus and working memory), and impacting visual comfort (via glare factors and color rendering).

findings.mechanism: LED lighting offers innovative features, energy efficiency, color control, longevity, and benefits on circadian rhythm regulation, emotional responses, cognitive performance, and visual comfort.
findings.quote: LED lighting demonstrates superiority over fluorescent lighting in enhancing worker performance and productivity due to its innovative features
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.antecedent: Spectral composition of artificial lighting (particularly blue light content)
findings.consequent: Melatonin suppression and circadian rhythm disruption
findings.mechanism: Influences internal biological clocks governing sleep-wake cycles and melatonin regulation, crucial for healthy sleep patterns.
findings.quote: Circadian rhythms... are profoundly influenced by the spectral composition of artificial lighting... blue light content, influences melatonin suppression
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.mechanism: Psychological impact on mood and emotional responses.
findings.quote: The effects extend to mood and emotional responses, as different lighting types can evoke varying emotional states, from relaxation to alertness
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.mechanism: Interference with melatonin regulation and circadian rhythms.
findings.quote: The quality of sleep is also intricately linked to lighting, as improper lighting conditions can disrupt sleep patterns and lead to sleep disturbances
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.quote: cognitive performance and concentration are heavily influenced by lighting types, with appropriate illumination enhancing focus and productivity
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.consequent: Eye strain, visual discomfort, hampered task engagement, diminished productivity
findings.mechanism: Direct impact on the visual system and cognitive resources.
findings.quote: inadequate lighting can lead to eye strain and visual discomfort, hampering task engagement... diminished productivity.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.consequent: Psychological implications (cooler lighting → alertness; warmer lighting → relaxation)
findings.mechanism: Association of color temperature with warmth/coolness and its psychological effects.
findings.quote: CCT... holds psychological implications, with cooler lighting promoting alertness and warmer lighting evoking relaxation
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.consequent: Alertness, mood, and overall experience (well-being and performance)
findings.mechanism: Adaptability and responsiveness to human needs, aligning with natural light cycles.
findings.quote: dynamic lighting, capable of mimicking natural light patterns, holds the potential to positively influence alertness, mood, and overall experience
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.mechanism: Potential overstimulation or disruption of natural light perception.
findings.quote: increasing maintained illuminance did not lead to positive results and resulted in negative effects on sleepiness, vitality, and mood.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Peeters et al. [18] findings.

findings.antecedent: Autonomous intelligent lighting systems (adapting to human emotions)
findings.mechanism: Elimination of distractions from manual configuration and personalized adaptation.
findings.quote: highlights the potential benefits of autonomous intelligent lighting systems... positive impact on productivity, health, and well-being.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Cupkova et al. [4] findings.

findings.mechanism: Optimization of visual comfort and cognitive engagement.
findings.quote: Benedetti et al. [3] explore the optimization of dynamic lighting control, revealing its positive influence on alertness and cognitive performance.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Benedetti et al. [3] findings.

findings.antecedent: Higher illuminance levels and higher CCT
findings.consequent: Increased alertness and positive affect in-office users
findings.quote: higher illuminance levels and higher CCT may contribute to increased alertness and positive affect in-office users.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of empirical studies in the review.

findings.antecedent: Both higher (1000 lx) and lower (200 lx) illuminance values (compared to 500 lx)
findings.mechanism: Potential for overstimulation or under-stimulation, affecting cognitive workload.
findings.quote: both higher (1000 lx) and lower (200 lx) illuminance values have a detrimental effect on work engagement
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Deng et al. [5] findings.

findings.antecedent: LED lighting with cooler colour temperatures
findings.quote: significant increase in subjective and objective alertness levels under LED lighting with cooler colour temperatures
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Kazemi et al. [11] findings.

findings.consequent: Physiological and ocular responses (Pupil Diameter, Pupillary Unrest Index, Blink Rate, Blink Amplitude, Eye Fixation Rate, Eye Convergence)
findings.mechanism: Direct impact on visual comfort and the visual system.
findings.quote: glare factors... can predict physiological and ocular responses, such as Pupil Diameter (PD), Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI)
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Hamedani et al. [6] findings.

findings.antecedent: Improved lighting environment (including sufficient light levels)
findings.consequent: Occupants' perception of fatigue levels, efficiency, and productivity at work
findings.mechanism: Enhanced visual comfort and cognitive support.
findings.quote: new interactive LED lighting improved workers' overall productivity and efficiency and reduced fatigue.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Synthesis of Kim et al. [12] findings.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The effects of artificial lighting on human behavior are generalizable across diverse populations, including larger and more diverse groups of at least 30 participants from various ages, genders, and occupations.

The impact of specific lighting design parameters (e.g., CCT, illuminance) and temporal variables (e.g., morning vs. afternoon) on human behavior can be independently measured and will show distinct effects.
Lighting glare and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) significantly influence human visual comfort and performance in office settings.
Multi-factorial lighting designs optimized for human-centered outcomes will lead to superior task performance compared to single-factor or non-optimized designs.
bridge_warrants: The review connects artificial lighting characteristics to chronobiological regulation, specifically circadian rhythms and melatonin suppression.
It links lighting to neuromodulatory systems by discussing its influence on mood, alertness, and emotional responses.
The paper bridges lighting design to cognitive performance and attention dynamics, suggesting impacts on focus, working memory, and task engagement.
It implicitly connects lighting to predictive processing through discussions of visual comfort, glare, and the perception of light quality.
methodological_critiques: Many reviewed studies suffered from small sample sizes and limited participant diversity, hindering the generalizability of findings.
Issues were identified with evaluation methods and data analysis, such as the use of Digital ID raising privacy concerns.
Experimental techniques and model approaches in some studies were limited, for instance, by not accounting for temporal variables like morning versus afternoon effects on working memory.
Some studies lacked a clear distinction between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements.
There is a need for deeper research into the impact of lighting glare and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) on human behaviour.
model_structure: The paper implicitly presents a conceptual model where various artificial lighting parameters (type, illuminance, CCT, glare, CRI, dynamic patterns) act as antecedents, influencing human physiological (circadian rhythms, ocular responses), psychological (mood, emotional states), and cognitive (alertness, focus, working memory) mechanisms, which in turn lead to consequents such as worker productivity, well-being, and health outcomes in office environments.
limitations: Gaps persist in sample sizes, participant diversity, evaluation methods, and data analysis across existing research.
Ethical considerations and experimental design issues require further addressing in future studies.
Unexplored factors like lighting glare and the Colour Rendering Index (CRI) represent avenues for further investigation.

Future research could benefit from broadening the scope to include other types of academic work (e.g., doctoral dissertations, research reports) and utilizing more specialized databases (e.g., Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, PubMed).

paper_metadata.title: Biophilia Upscaling: A Systematic Literature Review Based on a Three-Metric Approach
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Biophilia Upscaling: A Systematic Literature Review Based on a Three-Metric Approach
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In response to socio-ecological challenges, cities around the world are implementing greenification and urban forestry. While these strategies contribute to reducing the ecological footprint, they often overlook various social implications. This explains the increasing global attention to Biophilia, which emphasizes human–nature interaction to enhance the quality of urban life. Despite its historical roots spanning centuries, Biophilia is still considered an emerging research field, as shown by debate on evidence-based research and measurement of its multidimensional impacts. Although the beneficial effects of Biophilic Design (BD) are well documented thanks to the small-scale and immediate outcomes, the long-term potential of Biophilic Urbanism (BU) offers less evidence, limiting its utilization and investment. This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical-practical framework on Biophilia, BD, and BU through a 60-year systematic literature review based on a three-metric approach (quality, quantity, and application). Investigating concepts and practices, we delve into biophilic effects on humans and urban livability, analyze tools to measure them, and explore methods to translate them into the built environment. In spite of the growing body of studies and advancements in the last decade, our review findings highlight the need for further insights, especially regarding BU. The study aims to promote Biophilia Upscaling as a strategy to maximize its direct and indirect benefits across urban scales, thereby promoting BU and expediting a paradigm shift in city planning. In metropolises conceived as bioregional systems, where nature plays a key role in ensuring ecological services and citizens’ well-being, BU can assist designers, planners, and city makers in addressing the urban agenda toward higher environmental and social standards.
